title: Events & Tourism
tagline: Event planners, travel agents, and tour guides — crafting experiences people remember.
summary: Events and tourism turn logistics into memories: meeting and wedding planners, travel advisors, tour guides, and destination marketers. This roadmap covers the planning craft (budgets, vendors, day-of execution), the travel-advisor path, certifications, and building an experience business.

BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: The experience economy spans event planning (weddings, corporate, conferences), travel advising, tour operations, and venue/destination work — detail-obsessed, people-forward careers.
detail.why: Experience businesses reward organization and taste equally, hire from any background, and scale from freelance to agency.

Attend one wedding or corporate event as an observer

tasks: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities of an organization or department that serves the public, organizes events, or provides lodging and related services.

detail.description: Planners design and execute events in place; travel advisors design journeys across places; tour guides deliver them live. The skills overlap — logistics, vendors, and reading people.
detail.why: Knowing which craft you want determines your portfolio, certifications, and first clients.
learn: Compare the day-to-day of each role honestly
Shadow one planner and one guide if possible

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: The universal craft: timelines backward from the date, budgets with contingency lines, vendor coordination, and checklists that assume nothing.
detail.why: Experience businesses fail on logistics, not creativity — foundational discipline is the moat.

Draft a budget with 10% contingency
Run a vendor-communication tracker

detail.description: Events are emotional for clients: listening to visions, translating them to budgets, managing family/stakeholder dynamics, and staying calm when things break.
detail.why: Clients hire calm. Composure plus empathy is the actual product in weddings, galas, and tours alike.
learn: Practice the vision-intake conversation
Role-play a budget disappointment kindly
Learn a vendor-conflict de-escalation script
Build your 'things will go wrong' recovery kit

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: Each event type has its own economics and rhythm: weddings (emotional, high-touch), corporate (structured, repeatable), conferences (scale and AV), galas (fundraising), social parties.
detail.why: Specialists charge more and refer less competition — pick a type to master first.
learn: Compare run-of-show complexity across three types
Note which type matches your temperament
Study one type's vendor ecosystem
Choose your specialty

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: The money craft: allocation templates, vendor quotes and contracts, payment schedules, insurance requirements, and the negotiation that protects both sides.
detail.why: Budget mastery is why planners get rehired — overspend once and the reputation follows.
learn: Build a category allocation template (venue, F&B, AV, decor)
Read a vendor contract for hidden fees
Learn deposit and cancellation norms
Negotiate one mock vendor package

detail.description: Site craft: venue scouting, floor plans, capacity and fire codes, load-in/load-out, AV and power needs, accessibility, and the run-of-show that choreographs it all.
detail.why: Logistics fluency is what separates planners from decorators — it's the promotable skill.
learn: Tour 3 venues and note their constraints
Draft a run-of-show to 15-minute resolution
Learn load-in/load-out scheduling
Build an accessibility checklist

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: The live craft: directing vendors, managing timelines, handling guests, absorbing surprises invisibly, and closing out with teardown and settlements.
detail.why: Day-of composure is what clients remember and refer — it is the audition for every future contract.
learn: Coordinate one real event as second/assistant
Practice the invisible-fix mindset (no drama)
Build an emergency kit and vendor phone tree
Debrief every event: what broke, what saved it

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: Wedding planning is the best-known specialty: full-service vs month-of coordination, family dynamics, vendor dreams vs budgets, and a 12-month planning arc.
detail.why: Weddings are the highest-emotion, highest-referral niche — a portfolio of three good ones launches a business.
learn: Learn the 12-month wedding planning arc
Practice family-dynamics conversations
Build a preferred-vendor list for one venue
Offer month-of coordination to build reviews

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: Corporate events run on objectives and ROI: conferences with registration and AV, product launches, retreats, and repeatable annual budgets — steadier than weddings.
detail.why: Corporate clients rebook annually — one good conference relationship can fund a year.
learn: Learn registration and attendee-tracking basics
Understand AV/production terminology
Draft a conference run-of-show
Ask a corporate planner about sponsor sales

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: Modern travel advisors are designers and advocates: itineraries, supplier relationships (cruises, tours, resorts), commissions from suppliers, and troubleshooting when travel breaks.
detail.why: The advisor profession rebuilt itself post-internet by selling expertise and service — complex trips are back in demand.
learn: Compare host-agency vs independent advisor models
Learn commission structures (suppliers pay advisors)
Pick a specialization: honeymoons, groups, adventure
Take a supplier's free agent-training program

detail.description: Guides deliver experiences live: storytelling, group management, pacing, safety, and local depth — walking tours, museums, adventure, and multi-day coach tours.
detail.why: Guiding is the fastest entry into tourism (often seasonal) and the best public-speaking training money can't buy.
learn: Write and rehearse a 10-minute walking tour
Learn group-management and safety basics
Get first-aid certification if leading actively
Collect guest feedback after every tour

detail.description: The trade's tools: consumer booking sites (for research), agency platforms, CRM and itinerary builders, and registration/RSVP systems for events.
detail.why: Advisors and planners run on systems — the right stack makes one person look like a team.
learn: Trial 2 itinerary-builder or event platforms
Learn one registration/RSVP system end-to-end
Automate your client intake and proposals
Keep client data organized and private

detail.description: The recognized credentials: CMP (Events Industry Council, for experienced planners), CTA-style travel credentials (The Travel Institute), and destination-specialist courses from tourism boards.
detail.why: Certifications open corporate RFPs and supplier trust — most require experience first, so plan them at the right stage.
learn: Check CMP eligibility (experience-heavy) for later
Explore The Travel Institute's entry credentials now
Take a destination-specialist course for your niche
Track CE requirements if certified

certs.name: CMP
certs.note: Certified Meeting Professional — requires substantial documented event experience plus an exam.

detail.description: Going independent: legal structure, contracts and liability insurance, pricing (flat fee vs percentage vs commission), and a portfolio that sells before you do.
detail.why: Independence is the field's wealth path — the planners and advisors who systemize early own the businesses later.
learn: Register the business and get liability insurance
Build a contract template with a lawyer's review
Price your first year conservatively
Collect testimonials from every client

detail.description: Your proof is visual and verbal: photo galleries, styled-shoot participation, video snippets, and honest reviews on the platforms your clients actually check.
detail.why: Experience businesses sell trust — a strong portfolio converts strangers into inquiries without ads.
learn: Shoot every event professionally (hire or trade)
Publish 3 case studies: challenge, choices, outcome
Ask for reviews at the emotional peak
Refresh your portfolio quarterly

detail.description: Destinations have professional sides too: convention & visitors bureaus (DMOs), tourism boards, and hotels' own event-sales teams — salaried roles in the same ecosystem.
detail.why: DMO and hotel-sales roles offer the sector with a salary — and make you the person planners call.
learn: Find your local DMO and follow their work
Explore hotel event-sales career pages
Learn how DMOs court meeting planners
Offer to help host a familiarization tour

detail.description: Planner ladder: coordinator → planner → senior → director of events or agency owner. Travel ladder: advisor → specialty advisor → agency owner. Guides grow into tour operators.
detail.why: The experience economy rewards reputation compounding — every well-run event or trip is a seed for the next tier.
learn: Map the ladder for your lane with real postings
Choose year-one focus: skill depth or client volume
Find a mentor one tier ahead
Set a 3-year revenue or role goal

resources.title: BLS OOH — Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners

detail.description: Weddings cluster in warm months, conferences follow fiscal calendars, tourism peaks seasonally — income arrives in waves, so planning and saving are professional skills.
detail.why: The field's biggest survival error is treating peak-season income as steady income.
learn: Map your market's season calendar
Price peak work to carry the valleys
Build 3–6 months of reserves
Develop an off-season product (planning, consulting)

detail.description: Responsible experience design: crowd safety, weather and emergency plans, dietary and accessibility inclusion, and travel advisories — invisible when done right, catastrophic when ignored.
detail.why: One safety failure ends an experience business; inclusion and safety are now buying criteria.
learn: Build an emergency-action plan per event/tour
Get first-aid/CPR certified
Learn accessibility-inclusive design basics
Follow official travel advisories for clients

detail.description: Sustainable practice is now standard: waste reduction, local sourcing, carbon-conscious travel choices, and honest measurement — clients and venues increasingly require it.
detail.why: Sustainability literacy wins corporate RFPs and differentiates weddings and tours alike.
learn: Learn waste-reduction options per event type
Practice sourcing local vendors first
Measure one event's waste honestly
Market improvements factually, not as greenwash
